chunks.content: INTRODUCTION Idiopathic inflammatory myopathies (IIM) encompass a heterogeneous group of autoimmune disorders impacting multiple organs and systems, including muscles, skin, lungs, and joints [ ]. Dermatomyositis (DM), a prominent phenotype within IIM, is notably associated with cancer. Epidemiological studies define cancer-associated myositis as the occurrence of both cancer and myositis within a 3-year period [ ]. The exact mechanisms linking cancer and myositis remain unclear; however, previous research in DM and related autoimmune diseases, such as scleroderma, suggests that somatic mutations in the tumours of these patients may contribute to disease pathogenesis [ – ]. Early studies on patients with paraneoplastic systemic sclerosis, characterised by inflammation in the skin and other organs driven by DNA-directed RNA polymerase III subunit RPC1 (anti-RPC1) autoantibodies, suggest a molecular mechanism whereby tumour cells somatic mutations in the POLR3A gene, which encodes the RPC1 protein, lead to the formation of highly immunogenic neoantigens [ ]. These neoantigens trigger the production of antibodies that cross-react with nontumoural tissues, leading to autoimmune manifestations characteristic of the disease. In addition to POLR3A mutations, other tumours in patients with anti-RPC1-related scleroderma, however, did not exhibit somatic mutations; instead, they showed loss of heterozygosity (LOH) in the POLR3A locus [ ], a well-known phenomenon that results in the loss of the mutated allele—and consequently, the loss of expression of the associated neoantigen—thereby promoting immune evasion. Since this foundational study, advancements in understanding the genetic and immunological mechanisms underlying paraneoplastic diseases have remained limited. We recently reported that tumours from patients with cancer-associated dermatomyositis (CAD) and anti-TIF1γ autoantibodies harboured somatic mutations and LOH in the TIF1γ-related gene, tripartite motif containing 33 (TRIM33) [ ]. However, the prevalence of such alterations in TRIM33—as well as in other genes encoding known myositis autoantigens, including TRIM66, MORC3, chromodomain helicase DNA binding protein 4 (CHD4), and IFIH1 (corresponding to the anti-NXP2, anti-Mi-2, and antimelanoma differentiation-associated gene 5 protein [MDA5] autoantibodies, respectively)—is still poorly characterised. Moreover, no comprehensive multiomics studies have been conducted in CAD, and the underlying molecular mechanisms driving disease pathogenesis remain largely unexplored. Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have changed the land-scape of cancer, mainly in melanoma and nonsmall cell lung cancer among other tumours. These monoclonal antibodies activate the immune system increasing the immune reaction against tumour cells. Patients with autoimmune disorders are currently excluded from receiving such therapies to avoid potential immune-related adverse events (irAEs) and worsening of the preexisting autoimmune condition. However, clinical data show ICIs as efficacious antitumor therapy to patients with common autoimmune disorders while causing frequent but only mild and controllable irAEs [ , ]. Despite the extensive review of clinical and therapeutic data and outcome, the molecular basis of these clinically relevant questions remains largely unexplored and an in-depth investigation into the underlying molecular features that could drive response and/or irAEs remain lacking. In this study, we aim to build upon our previous findings by performing integrated genomic, transcriptomic, and immunophenotypic analyses of both tumoural and nontumoural tissues from patients with CAD. METHODS Patients Fifteen patients diagnosed with CAD at Vall d’Hebron University Hospital were included in the study. The diagnosis of DM was based on both the European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology / American College of Rheumatology (EULAR/ACR) criteria (score >95) [ ] and the European Neuromuscular Centre (ENMC) criteria [ ]. Serum samples were tested for anti-MDA5, anti-small ubiquitin-like modifier activating enzyme (antiSAE), anti-Mi2, and anti-NXP2 autoantibodies using a commercial immunoblot assay (Euroimmun, Lübeck, Germany), and for anti-TIF1γ using an in-house blot/Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay (ELISA) previously validated by immunoprecipitation [ ]. Biological samples A total of 38 biological samples from the 15 patients with CAD were available for multi-OMICs profiling and immunophenotyping. These included 15 tumour samples, 6 muscle lesions, and 2 skin lesions and 15 germline DNA. From these specimens, we generated whole-exome sequencing data (N = 33). Additionally, a subset of samples underwent whole-genome sequencing (N = 8), RNA sequencing (N = 6), and immunophenotyping (N = 12) for comprehensive immunogenomic profiling ( ; ). DNA was sequenced in paired-end format using NovaSeq instrumentation (Illumina) to a coverage depth of ≥300×. SNVs were stratified by their false-positive likelihood using the variant quality score recalibration module (GATK), in addition to inhouse SNV accuracy software. Miscalled variants were omitted using in-house SNV accuracy software, which employs a model informed by genomic context and sequence alignment data. MuTect [ ] was used to call somatic SNVs and indels, and Var-dict [ ] was used to call small somatic insertions or deletions (indels) less than 50 bp. Combined somatic SNV and indel calls were then analysed through a set of rigorously validated filters incorporating coverage, read quality, and positional features, along with the likelihood of presence in normal tissue. We calculated the P value for observing the number of somatic mutations detected or a higher count using a Poisson-binomial distribution Discrete Fourier Transform and Convolutional Fast Fourier Transform (DFT-CFFTDFT-CFFT), with individual mutation probabilities derived from the somatic genetic variants identified in the 10,967 tumour samples of the Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) PanCancer Atlas Study [ ]. Copy number analysis and clonality estimation Allele-specific copy number analysis of tumors (ASCAT) (v3.1.3) was used to identify which regions of the tumour genome have gained or lost gene copies, while adjusting for tumour purity and ploidy. This algorithm accurately dissects allele-specific copy number profiles in solid tumours by accounting for tumour cellularity and nonaberrant (normal) cell admixture [ ]. As a result, it allows for precise detection of genomic gains, losses, copy number-neutral events, and LOH. Clonality of somatic mutations was assessed by calculating the cancer cell fraction (CCF), which indicates whether a given mutation is present in all tumour cells (clonal) or only in a subset (subclonal). This distinction provides valuable insights into the evolutionary dynamics and potential aggressiveness of the tumour. CCF was estimated using the formula: CCF = VAF/(P·CT + (1—P)·CN), where VAF is the variant allele frequency, P is tumour purity, CT is the copy number at the mutation site in the tumour, and CN is the corresponding copy number in normal tissue (typically assumed to be 2 for autosomes). Variants with CCF > 0.9 were considered clonal, whereas those below this threshold were classified as subclonal. Typing and LOH of HLA loci Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA) typing up to 4 places was carried out via the ImmunoID NeXT Platform, which employs probes targeting the Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC) reference sequences in the GRCh38 human reference genome. HLA LOH was called using DASH (Deletion of Allele-Specific HLAs), a machine-learning-based algorithm [ ]. Neoantigen prediction Nonsynonymous somatic DNA variants (SNVs, indels, and fusions) were used to call putative neoantigens, which were then verified using transcriptomic data. For each putative neoantigen, all peptides containing the event were generated; binding was assessed for each Class I HLA using NetMHC [ ] and NetMHCpan [ ], and immunogenecity scores were calculated as described in Calis et al [ ]. RNA sequencing Whole transcriptome sequencing of tumour RNA was performed as described in Abbott et al. Briefly, RNA sequencing was performed to a coverage depth of ≥192 million reads, with augmentation of T-cell receptor (TCR) regions (100-fold). Ribosomal reads were excluded, and transcripts were aligned using STAR [ ]. Transcript expression was calculated and normalised with the aid of Salmon [ ], and gene expression was derived using a proprietary tool, Expressionist (Personalis, Inc). TCR sequencing TCR β clones were profiled using the ImmunoID NeXT RepertoireID. RepertoireID captures CDR3 regions and boosts TCR region transcriptome sequencing to over 100 times the standard ImmunoID NeXT transcriptome. TCR clones were identified using MiXCR. Clones containing frameshift mutations or premature stop codons in the CDR3 sequence were omitted, along with clones with alignment scores below 70 for V or J sequences. Regarding tumour type, 6 patients (40%) were diagnosed with thoracic malignancies (5 small-cell lung cancer [SCLC], and 1 thymic carcinoma), 3 patients with gynaecological malignancies (1 squamous cervix carcinoma, 1 cervix adenocarcinoma, and 1 ovarian serous carcinoma), and 3 patients with gastrointestinal malignancies (1 colonic neuroendocrine tumour-NET, 1 rectum adenocarcinoma, and 1 stomach adenocarcinoma). Two patients presented with breast cancer, and 1 patient presented nasopharyngeal carcinoma ( ). Two patients had localised tumours, and 1 patient was diagnosed with DM in a malignancy relapse. Data on patients’ cancer diagnoses, immunological profiles, and the timing of DM onset in relation to cancer diagnosis and treatment are summarised in . Our analyses revealed a spectrum of mutations, copy number alterations (CNA), and gene fusions ( ) in cancer-associated genes listed on the OncoKB platform [ ]. The tumour sample from patient DM8, who was diagnosed with SCLC and detectable TIF1γ circulating antibodies, had a somatic mutation in TRIM33 (p. Y1072), a mutation previously linked to CAM [ ] ( ). Also, patient DM16, who was diagnosed with stomach adenocarcinoma and detectable TIF1γ circulating antibodies, had another somatic mutation in TRIM33 (p.R440C). Tumours from other patients with anti-TIF1γ autoantibodies (DM1, DM12, DM17, DM18, and DM19) presented evidence of LOH in the TRIM33, TRIM24, and TRIM66 genes ( , ), which together with the TRIM33 , TRIM24 , and TRIM28 forms the transcriptional intermediary factor 1 (TIF1) family proteins [ ] ( ). Patient DM15, who presented anti-NXP2 autoantibodies, was found to have a somatic mutation in MORC3 , the gene encoding the NXP2 protein, and LOH in Microrchidia family CW-type zinc finger 2 ( MORC2 ) ( ), a gene closely related structurally to MORC3 ( , ). Similarly, patient DM4, with anti-Mi2 autoantibodies presented focal amplifications in chromosome 12 that contains the CHD4 gene, coding for Mi2b ( ). Patient DM3, with anti-SAE autoantibodies, presented a gain in the whole chromosome 19, the genomic region that contains the gene UMO1 Activating Enzyme Subunit 1 ( SAE1 ) ( ). Lastly, patient DM2, who tested positive for antibodies against MDA5, was diagnosed with nasopharyngeal carcinoma that exhibited a previously unreported missense somatic mutation (p.D408H) in the gene encoding interferon-induced helicase C domain-containing protein 1 ( IFIH1 ), which is responsible for producing MDA5 ( ). As an indirect assessment of LOH in DM-associated genes, we compared the mutant allele frequencies (MAF) between the 2 cohorts. A high somatic MAF is indicative of LOH. The average MAF of tumours from the DM cohort ( – ) was 0.75 (75%), suggestive of frequent LOH, whereas the average MAF in 1128 non-DM tumours was significantly lower (31%, t-test P < .001), suggesting that LOH is rare in this context. Specifically, only 2.5% of non-DM tumours exhibited a MAF higher than 0.59, which was the minimum observed among DM-associated tumours ( ). To further assess the likelihood of observing somatic mutations in autoantigen-encoding genes among patients with CAD, we compared the observed mutation frequency with the expected background mutation risk. Across the analysed cases, somatic mutations were identified in 4 out of 12 tumours in genes corresponding to known autoantibodies. Using reported baseline mutation frequencies for each gene, we calculated a cumulative P value of 1.3 × 10 −5 . Clonality of somatic mutations in cancer-associated DM-related genes To determine when the IFIH1 and TRIM33 mutations occurred during tumorigenesis, we calculated the CCF based on variant allele frequency, copy number, and ploidy, as detailed in the section. The CCF values for both IFIH1 and TRIM33 mutations were 1, strongly indicating that these mutations arose early, likely during tumour initiation. These findings are consistent with the co-occurrence of common driver mutations such as TP53, CSM3 , and KMT2D , all of which also exhibited CCF values greater than 0.9, in line with their role in early tumorigenesis ( ). Analysis of genetic events in paired paraneoplastic lesions and tumours We conducted whole-exome sequencing (WES) on genomic DNA (gDNA) and paired tumour and muscle paraneoplastic lesions in 6 patients with CAD. Employing a stringent MAF cutoff of 5%, we detected somatic mutations in all sequenced muscle samples. The median number of mutations was 9.2 (ranging from 5 to 15) and a MAF ranging from 5% to 44% ( ). The number of mutations observed in affected muscle lesions was significantly lower than that in tumours, with the number of mutations in tumours ranging from 297 to 2309 and MAFs from 5% to 98% ( ). Importantly, no genetic events at the mutation or gene level were shared between paired tumour and muscle lesions from the same patient, except for a single instance where the FAM47B , a gene with largely unknown functions, carried mutations in both the tumour (p.P25L, MAF = 32%) and muscle (p.H246P, MAF = 6%) ( ). HLA typing HLA typing at the germinal level was performed on all patients, and there was no enrichment of a specific typing in our cohort ( – ). Somatic HLA allele-specific copy number was also analysed, and one tumour showed evidence of LOH in the tumour sample from patient DM3 ( ). Immune profiling in tumours We characterised tumour-infiltration lymphocytes in 10 tumours by sequential multiplexed immunohistochemistry and grouped lesions into different categories according to the density of immune cells and the pattern of infiltration ( , ). Two tumours were defined as ‘hot/inflamed’ based on a substantial intratumoural and peritumoral infiltration of T cells; 4 tumours were classified as ‘excluded’, indicating the presence of a considerable number of T cells at the interface between the tumour and peritumoral stroma but relatively few within the tumours themselves; another 4 tumours, all SCLCs, were categorised as ‘desert’, revealing a very low or complete absence of T cells both outside and inside the tumours ( – ). Immune profiling in skin paraneoplastic lesions Immunophenotyping and RNAseq deconvolution analyses unveiled elevated infiltration of immune cells in the 2 skin lesions available for the study, from patients DM5 and DM10 ( , and – ). TCR-seq repertoire in tumours and skin paraneoplastic lesions In our RNAseq data analysis, we observed significant variability in the TCR repertoire across both skin lesions and tumours. Approximately, half of the samples exhibited increased clonality, while the other half displayed a multitude of clones with relatively low frequencies ( ). Particularly striking was the divergent TCR repertoire in the paired skin lesion and tumour of patient DM5. The skin lesion exhibited a plethora of TCR clones (N = 106) with notably low frequencies (average 0.009, range 8e-5-0.049), whereas the tumour demonstrated a markedly lower number of TCR clones (N = 50) but with considerably higher frequencies (average 0.02, range 0.001-0.284). Importantly, 6 TCRs were shared between the skin and the tumour. Remarkably, all 6 of these TCRs were substantially enriched in the tumour, ranging from 4.16 to 45.35 times ( – ). DISCUSSION This study reveals a high prevalence of genetic alterations in tumour cells affecting genes that encode DM-specific autoantigens in patients with CAD. These genetic alterations are exceedingly rare in databases like TCGA [ ] and GENIE [ ], suggesting that they could be specific to CAD. These findings suggest that such tumour-specific alterations may play a central role in initiating the autoimmune response, potentially through the generation of neoantigens that drive the production of myositis-specific autoantibodies. In addition, the identification of distinct immunogenomic profiles and tumour-infiltrating lymphocyte patterns provides further insight into the immunopathogenesis of CAD and supports a model of paraneoplastic autoimmunity driven by early oncogenic events. In total, genetic alterations in CAD-related genes were highly frequent (75%), strongly suggesting that such genetic alterations may serve as the initiating pathogenic basis of the disease. This finding parallels the high frequency of POLR3A mutations and LOH observed in tumours from patients with scleroderma paraneoplastic disease and anti-RPC1 antibodies (75%) [ ]. Interestingly, we identified somatic mutations in autoantigens corresponding to the detected autoantibodies in patient groups not typically associated with cancer, with anti-MDA5 serving as a notable example. Although most patients with anti-MDA5 DM are not paraneoplastic and our cohort overall did not demonstrate a strong association between anti-MDA5 autoantibodies and cancer, this particular patient exhibited a clear cancer association and harboured a mutation in the relevant autoantigen. These findings suggest that distinct sources of molecular mimicry may give rise to the same autoantibody. We propose that in most patients from cancer-unrelated groups, such as anti-MDA5, autoantibodies emerge through molecular mimicry triggered by noncancer sources, including viral or bacterial antigens. By contrast, in a minority of patients—such as the case described here—they may instead result from tumour-derived mutations that generate neoantigens. For autoantibodies strongly associated with malignancy, such as anti-TIF1γ, the balance of mechanisms may be shifted towards tumour-derived sources, translating into an epidemiological association with cancer. Based on the results in this study and previous research from our group and others, the current model of CAD disease suggests that tumour neoantigens induce myositis-specific antibodies (MSA) against the mutated neoantigen that then cross-react with the unmutated antigens found in other tissues, such as skin or muscle [ ]. Consistent with this model, we identified somatic genetic events in CAD-specific genes such as TRIM33 and TRIM66 within the tumours. Importantly, our study extends this paradigm beyond anti-TIF1γ-positive patients by reporting, for the first time, a somatic mutation in the IFIH1 gene, which encodes the MDA5 protein, in a patient positive for anti-MDA5 antibodies (patient DM2, ), as well as a somatic mutation in MORC3 in a patient with anti-NXP2 autoantibodies. The new mutation in anti-MDA5 is predicted to result in the overproduction of IFN-gamma according to conformational and functional studies of MDA5 protein. It is worth noting that gain-of-function mutations in the IFIH1 MDA5 gene cause type 1 interferonopathies [ ]. Our findings underscore the potential significance of IFIH1 MDA5 mutations in triggering autoimmunity and in the development of CAD. Moreover, recently published findings indicate that certain autoantibodies in myositis can be internalised into living cells [ , ], where they disrupt the function of their respective autoantigens, providing further evidence for a self-perpetuating cycle of the disease, particularly in patients with CAD. In this cycle, somatic mutations in tumours generate neoantigens, which trigger the production of myositis-associated autoantibodies by the immune system. These autoantibodies subsequently are internalised, targeting the corresponding wild-type antigens in affected tissues and disrupting the function of theirrespective autoantigens, thereby contributing to the characteristic autoimmune manifestations of the disease. Our immunophenotyping analysis revealed heterogeneous immune infiltration patterns in tumours from patients with CAD, using T-cell (CD4, CD8, FOXP3), B-cell (CD20), and Programmed death-ligand 1 (PDL1) markers. As typical of autoimmune contexts, paraneoplastic lesions predominantly exhibited an ‘inflamed’ phenotype with dense immune infiltration ( ). TCR sequencing further demonstrated minimal clonal overlap between tumours and paraneoplastic lesions, suggesting a more selective T-cell infiltration in the tumour than in areas affected with paraneoplastic autoimmunity ( – and ). SCLC is an aggressively progressing cancer that is frequently associated with various paraneoplastic syndromes [ , ]. ICIs have gained approval for use in both first- and second-line treatments for SCLC [ , ]. Distinct immune profiles have been observed depending on the type of paraneoplastic syndrome. Notably, neurologic paraneoplastic syndromes were associated with higher CD3+ T-cell infiltration (88% vs 33%) and improved overall survival compared to endocrinologic cases, even under similar treatment regimens [ ]. In our small cohort of 4 patients with SCLC with CAD, tumours showed ‘cold’ immune phenotypes, lacking immune infiltration and PDL1 expression. Despite the risk of flare and irAEs, patients with preexisting common autoimmune disease can experience clinical benefit from ICI [ , ]. However, it is currently unclear whether patients with rare autoimmune diseases, such as CAD, could benefit from these treatments in a safe manner. Notwithstanding the limited number of patients included in our study, our immunophenotyping, RNAseq, and TCRseq data reveal that the immu- nogenomic profiles of the paraneoplastic lesions and tumours in the patients do not seem to greatly overlap but rather are composed of mutually exclusive somatic mutations and diverse TCR clones ( and ). This indicates that the autoimmune response to the muscle and skin, while likely triggered by genetic events at the tumour site, has evolved separately over time ( ). Taking into consideration the distinct immune profiles, we observed in tumour and nontumoural tissues, patients with CAD could possibly benefit from the anticancer benefits of ICI without necessarily eliciting a major flare in the paraneoplastic lesions at least in some cases. The present study, while offering valuable insights, must be interpreted within the context of its inherent limitations. Although this represents the largest cohort analysed at the molecular level to date, the modest sample size of 15 patients limits statistical power and constrains the generalisability of the findings. In addition, the expected mutation rates were derived from large publicly available datasets rather than sequencing data drawn from an identical epidemiologic background. Furthermore, the heterogeneous nature of the cancer types associated with CAD presents another natural limitation. The diverse range of cancer types, each with distinct molecular profiles and clinical characteristics, may introduce substantial variability in the results. Autoantibodies against TRIM24, TRIM28, and TRIM66—all members of the TIF1 family sharing relevant structural homology with TRIM33—were not tested, and these specificities were therefore excluded from the analysis assessing the association between cancer and myositis. The significance of these variants in relation to immune responses remains undetermined. Future research with larger independent cohorts of patients will be needed to validate our findings and generalise the observed outcomes. In conclusion, the current study reports the largest cohort of patients with CAM with available multiomics data described to date. The results define tumour mutations and/or genetic imbalance in genes that codify for antigenic proteins, leading to MSA as the genetic basis of CAD. Furthermore, our molecular findings demonstrating distinct immune profiles in tumour and nontumoural tissues may support future investigations into the use of ICI in patients with CAD. The comprehensive data analysis presented here reveals that tumours and paraneoplastic lesions in patients with CAD may harbour divergent genetic and immunological characteristics. These findings provide novel insights into the interplay between autoimmunity and tumour immunity in CAD, suggesting that while specific antigens may act as common triggers for the autoimmune response, the overall immunogenomic landscapes of these conditions remain largely distinct. This growing body of evidence supports the role of somatic mutations as potential initiators of autoimmune disease and may guide future investigations into the use of ICIs as a therapeutic strategy for patients with autoimmune disorders. However, clinical data show ICIs as efficacious antitumor therapy to patients with common autoimmune disorders while causing frequent but only mild and controllable irAEs [ , ]. The tumour sample from patient DM8, who was diagnosed with SCLC and detectable TIF1γ circulating antibodies, had a somatic mutation in TRIM33 (p. Y1072), a mutation previously linked to CAM [ ] ( ). Similarly, patient DM4, with anti-Mi2 autoantibodies presented focal amplifications in chromosome 12 that contains the CHD4 gene, coding for Mi2b ( ). Patient DM3, with anti-SAE autoantibodies, presented a gain in the whole chromosome 19, the genomic region that contains the gene UMO1 Activating Enzyme Subunit 1 ( SAE1 ) ( ). Across the analysed cases, somatic mutations were identified in 4 out of 12 tumours in genes corresponding to known autoantibodies. Using reported baseline mutation frequencies for each gene, we calculated a cumulative P value of 1.3 × 10 −5 . Clonality of somatic mutations in cancer-associated DM-related genes To determine when the IFIH1 and TRIM33 mutations occurred during tumorigenesis, we calculated the CCF based on variant allele frequency, copy number, and ploidy, as detailed in the section. The CCF values for both IFIH1 and TRIM33 mutations were 1, strongly indicating that these mutations arose early, likely during tumour initiation. These findings are consistent with the co-occurrence of common driver mutations such as TP53, CSM3 , and KMT2D , all of which also exhibited CCF values greater than 0.9, in line with their role in early tumorigenesis ( ). Employing a stringent MAF cutoff of 5%, we detected somatic mutations in all sequenced muscle samples. The median number of mutations was 9.2 (ranging from 5 to 15) and a MAF ranging from 5% to 44% ( ). The number of mutations observed in affected muscle lesions was significantly lower than that in tumours, with the number of mutations in tumours ranging from 297 to 2309 and MAFs from 5% to 98% ( ). Approximately, half of the samples exhibited increased clonality, while the other half displayed a multitude of clones with relatively low frequencies ( ). Particularly striking was the divergent TCR repertoire in the paired skin lesion and tumour of patient DM5. The skin lesion exhibited a plethora of TCR clones (N = 106) with notably low frequencies (average 0.009, range 8e-5-0.049), whereas the tumour demonstrated a markedly lower number of TCR clones (N = 50) but with considerably higher frequencies (average 0.02, range 0.001-0.284). Importantly, 6 TCRs were shared between the skin and the tumour. Remarkably, all 6 of these TCRs were substantially enriched in the tumour, ranging from 4.16 to 45.35 times ( – ). DISCUSSION This study reveals a high prevalence of genetic alterations in tumour cells affecting genes that encode DM-specific autoantigens in patients with CAD. These genetic alterations are exceedingly rare in databases like TCGA [ ] and GENIE [ ], suggesting that they could be specific to CAD. These findings suggest that such tumour-specific alterations may play a central role in initiating the autoimmune response, potentially through the generation of neoantigens that drive the production of myositis-specific autoantibodies. In addition, the identification of distinct immunogenomic profiles and tumour-infiltrating lymphocyte patterns provides further insight into the immunopathogenesis of CAD and supports a model of paraneoplastic autoimmunity driven by early oncogenic events. In total, genetic alterations in CAD-related genes were highly frequent (75%), strongly suggesting that such genetic alterations may serve as the initiating pathogenic basis of the disease. This finding parallels the high frequency of POLR3A mutations and LOH observed in tumours from patients with scleroderma paraneoplastic disease and anti-RPC1 antibodies (75%) [ ]. Interestingly, we identified somatic mutations in autoantigens corresponding to the detected autoantibodies in patient groups not typically associated with cancer, with anti-MDA5 serving as a notable example. Although most patients with anti-MDA5 DM are not paraneoplastic and our cohort overall did not demonstrate a strong association between anti-MDA5 autoantibodies and cancer, this particular patient exhibited a clear cancer association and harboured a mutation in the relevant autoantigen. These findings suggest that distinct sources of molecular mimicry may give rise to the same autoantibody. We propose that in most patients from cancer-unrelated groups, such as anti-MDA5, autoantibodies emerge through molecular mimicry triggered by noncancer sources, including viral or bacterial antigens. By contrast, in a minority of patients—such as the case described here—they may instead result from tumour-derived mutations that generate neoantigens. For autoantibodies strongly associated with malignancy, such as anti-TIF1γ, the balance of mechanisms may be shifted towards tumour-derived sources, translating into an epidemiological association with cancer. Based on the results in this study and previous research from our group and others, the current model of CAD disease suggests that tumour neoantigens induce myositis-specific antibodies (MSA) against the mutated neoantigen that then cross-react with the unmutated antigens found in other tissues, such as skin or muscle [ ]. Consistent with this model, we identified somatic genetic events in CAD-specific genes such as TRIM33 and TRIM66 within the tumours. Importantly, our study extends this paradigm beyond anti-TIF1γ-positive patients by reporting, for the first time, a somatic mutation in the IFIH1 gene, which encodes the MDA5 protein, in a patient positive for anti-MDA5 antibodies (patient DM2, ), as well as a somatic mutation in MORC3 in a patient with anti-NXP2 autoantibodies. The new mutation in anti-MDA5 is predicted to result in the overproduction of IFN-gamma according to conformational and functional studies of MDA5 protein. It is worth noting that gain-of-function mutations in the IFIH1 MDA5 gene cause type 1 interferonopathies [ ]. Our findings underscore the potential significance of IFIH1 MDA5 mutations in triggering autoimmunity and in the development of CAD. Moreover, recently published findings indicate that certain autoantibodies in myositis can be internalised into living cells [ , ], where they disrupt the function of their respective autoantigens, providing further evidence for a self-perpetuating cycle of the disease, particularly in patients with CAD. Our findings underscore the potential significance of IFIH1 MDA5 mutations in triggering autoimmunity and in the development of CAD. Moreover, recently published findings indicate that certain autoantibodies in myositis can be internalised into living cells [ , ], where they disrupt the function of their respective autoantigens, providing further evidence for a self-perpetuating cycle of the disease, particularly in patients with CAD. In this cycle, somatic mutations in tumours generate neoantigens, which trigger the production of myositis-associated autoantibodies by the immune system. These autoantibodies subsequently are internalised, targeting the corresponding wild-type antigens in affected tissues and disrupting the function of theirrespective autoantigens, thereby contributing to the characteristic autoimmune manifestations of the disease. Our immunophenotyping analysis revealed heterogeneous immune infiltration patterns in tumours from patients with CAD, using T-cell (CD4, CD8, FOXP3), B-cell (CD20), and Programmed death-ligand 1 (PDL1) markers. As typical of autoimmune contexts, paraneoplastic lesions predominantly exhibited an ‘inflamed’ phenotype with dense immune infiltration ( ). TCR sequencing further demonstrated minimal clonal overlap between tumours and paraneoplastic lesions, suggesting a more selective T-cell infiltration in the tumour than in areas affected with paraneoplastic autoimmunity ( – and ). SCLC is an aggressively progressing cancer that is frequently associated with various paraneoplastic syndromes [ , ]. ICIs have gained approval for use in both first- and second-line treatments for SCLC [ , ]. Distinct immune profiles have been observed depending on the type of paraneoplastic syndrome. Notably, neurologic paraneoplastic syndromes were associated with higher CD3+ T-cell infiltration (88% vs 33%) and improved overall survival compared to endocrinologic cases, even under similar treatment regimens [ ]. In our small cohort of 4 patients with SCLC with CAD, tumours showed ‘cold’ immune phenotypes, lacking immune infiltration and PDL1 expression. Despite the risk of flare and irAEs, patients with preexisting common autoimmune disease can experience clinical benefit from ICI [ , ]. However, it is currently unclear whether patients with rare autoimmune diseases, such as CAD, could benefit from these treatments in a safe manner. Notwithstanding the limited number of patients included in our study, our immunophenotyping, RNAseq, and TCRseq data reveal that the immu- nogenomic profiles of the paraneoplastic lesions and tumours in the patients do not seem to greatly overlap but rather are composed of mutually exclusive somatic mutations and diverse TCR clones ( and ). This indicates that the autoimmune response to the muscle and skin, while likely triggered by genetic events at the tumour site, has evolved separately over time ( ). Taking into consideration the distinct immune profiles, we observed in tumour and nontumoural tissues, patients with CAD could possibly benefit from the anticancer benefits of ICI without necessarily eliciting a major flare in the paraneoplastic lesions at least in some cases. The present study, while offering valuable insights, must be interpreted within the context of its inherent limitations. Although this represents the largest cohort analysed at the molecular level to date, the modest sample size of 15 patients limits statistical power and constrains the generalisability of the findings. In addition, the expected mutation rates were derived from large publicly available datasets rather than sequencing data drawn from an identical epidemiologic background. Furthermore, the heterogeneous nature of the cancer types associated with CAD presents another natural limitation. The diverse range of cancer types, each with distinct molecular profiles and clinical characteristics, may introduce substantial variability in the results. Autoantibodies against TRIM24, TRIM28, and TRIM66—all members of the TIF1 family sharing relevant structural homology with TRIM33—were not tested, and these specificities were therefore excluded from the analysis assessing the association between cancer and myositis. The significance of these variants in relation to immune responses remains undetermined. Future research with larger independent cohorts of patients will be needed to validate our findings and generalise the observed outcomes. In conclusion, the current study reports the largest cohort of patients with CAM with available multiomics data described to date. The results define tumour mutations and/or genetic imbalance in genes that codify for antigenic proteins, leading to MSA as the genetic basis of CAD. Furthermore, our molecular findings demonstrating distinct immune profiles in tumour and nontumoural tissues may support future investigations into the use of ICI in patients with CAD. The comprehensive data analysis presented here reveals that tumours and paraneoplastic lesions in patients with CAD may harbour divergent genetic and immunological characteristics. These findings provide novel insights into the interplay between autoimmunity and tumour immunity in CAD, suggesting that while specific antigens may act as common triggers for the autoimmune response, the overall immunogenomic landscapes of these conditions remain largely distinct. This growing body of evidence supports the role of somatic mutations as potential initiators of autoimmune disease and may guide future investigations into the use of ICIs as a therapeutic strategy for patients with autoimmune disorders. chunks.content: Introduction Systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases (SARDs) can result in prolonged morbidity and substantial healthcare utilisation. , , Current data suggest that Australia has an above‐average prevalence of several SARDs , , , , , , , and possible geographic variation in prevalence, perhaps driven by environmental exposures , , , , , , , , , , Accurate national SARD prevalence estimates can inform healthcare system planning and establish reference points for identifying geographic or temporal clusters. This systematic literature review and meta‐analysis summarises available data on the Australian incidence or prevalence of multiple SARDs, specifically vasculitis (including ANCA‐associated vasculitis (AAV), Takayasu arteritis, giant cell arteritis (GCA), IgA vasculitis and Behcet disease), systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), rheumatoid arthritis (RA), systemic sclerosis (SSc), idiopathic inflammatory myopathies (IIM), spondyloarthritis (SpA), Sjogren disease (SjD) and mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD). Given their rarity and the challenges in diagnosis (evolving criteria, heterogenous disease manifestations), SARD prevalence estimates are difficult to obtain, and shared insights can be drawn from examining the methodologies used. Our objectives were to: (1) synthesise Australian studies of incidence or prevalence of the listed SARD, (2) generate pooled incidence or prevalence estimates where possible and (3) identify opportunities for future research. Methods Study design This study followed the Joanna Briggs Institute guidance for prevalence reviews, and reporting follows the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta‐Analyses (PRISMA) checklist. Eligibility criteria We included peer‐reviewed studies and grey literature published prior to July 2024 that: (1) involved Australian children or adults; (2) identified SARDs by self‐report, clinician diagnosis or administrative data; and (3) reported or provided sufficient data to calculate SARD incidence or prevalence. We excluded studies that: (1) reported SARD frequency only within specific conditions (i.e. pregnancy) , , and (2) were duplicate publications of identical data, including conference abstracts with a subsequent paper, literature reviews and secondary analyses of Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) National Health Surveys or Global Burden of Disease data. , , , Several studies had overlapping but non‐identical populations (e.g. same site, different years or case definitions). To avoid regional over‐representation, we performed sensitivity analyses comparing inclusion of one or both studies. Both were retained only if they shifted the pooled estimate in opposite directions or had minimal impact in the same direction (defined as <10% relative change, <2 per 100 000 absolute change and within the original 95% confidence interval (CI)). When only one was included, the more recent study was preferred. Where studies covered overlapping but highly distinct catchments (e.g. state‐wide vs single hospital , ), both were included. Information sources Medline, EMBASE, CINAHL, Web of Science, Scopus, Google Scholar and Google (to identify grey literature) databases were searched on 1 July 2024. The search strategy (Section ( )) was developed with an academic librarian. Selection process and data collection The first author (LR) screened all abstracts to exclude clearly non‐relevant articles, with the remainder moving to full text review. The full texts were independently screened by two authors (LR and EC or TY), with discrepancies resolved with the senior author (MN). Data from included studies were extracted into a template using Covidence software. Risk‐of‐bias assessment We assessed study quality using the Hoy Risk of Bias Tool, which is appropriate for prevalence studies and provides a summary score (0–9) and overall ratings of low, moderate or high risk of bias. Statistical analysis Studies were synthesised narratively, and key results are summarised in Sections . A meta‐analysis was performed when three or more studies reported on the same disease in comparable populations and were not high risk of bias. To account for potential differences in disease patterns, meta‐analyses were conducted separately for paediatric and adult populations. When reported denominators were descriptive (i.e. ‘population of South Australia’), population data from the ABS was used for model weighting. For studies reporting incidence rates without CIs or population data, these values were estimated assuming a Poisson distribution. Incidence and prevalence were standardised to cases per 100 000 person‐years and per 100 000 population, unless otherwise specified (vasculitis and IIM are reported per million due to rarity, and inflammatory arthritis is reported in percent due to high prevalence). Where disease definitions varied, results were disaggregated into comparable subgroups (e.g. IIM subtypes). To account for suspected regional differences and low prevalence data, a random‐effects model (with inverse variance weighting and Freeman‐Tukey double arcsine transformation) was applied to prevalence data. For diseases with incidence data, a random‐effects model was fitted to log‐transformed incidence data. If significant heterogeneity was present (identified by a wide prediction interval), a subgroup analysis was performed to investigate the cause. This approach has been recommended over the use of Tau2 or I 2 in prevalence or incidence meta‐analysis. , Studies reporting point or 5‐year period prevalence were included, as SARDs are chronic with stable incidence and mortality; both measures reflect the same underlying frequency. Sensitivity analyses showed that 5‐year estimates did not introduce heterogeneity. The influence of outlying results was assessed by sequentially excluding these studies in sensitivity analyses. The GRADE assessment was not applied as these were observational data. Certainty of evidence was assessed by considering risk of bias and heterogeneity. High‐risk studies were excluded from the meta‐analysis to improve confidence in the results. Rheumatoid arthritis Ten publications have examined RA prevalence in Australia (Section ); however, a meta‐analysis was not possible due to heterogeneity and study quality (Section ). Five editions of the National Health Survey (NHS) estimated RA prevalence at 2%–2.8% from 2009 to 2023 , , but relied on self‐report, which overestimates RA prevalence, leading to a high risk‐of‐bias rating. A 1999 South Australia (SA) survey identified an RA prevalence of 0.9%, based on self‐report of medically confirmed cases. There are four other studies of RA prevalence. First, a linked data analysis of the Australian Longitudinal Study of Women's Health (ALSWH) and administrative health data compared five case identification techniques, reporting a prevalence of 1.1%–5.4%, confirming that self‐report over‐estimates prevalence. Although rigorous, the study was not incorporated into the meta‐analysis as it only included women. The second study, conducted in Western Australia (WA), using hospital data and aggregated Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS) data, estimated RA prevalence at 0.34%–0.72% for 1995–2014. These estimates were lower than those from the ALSWH study, likely due to stricter medication definitions and inclusion of males. The authors assumed that 50% of RA patients use biologic disease‐modifying antirheumatic drugs (bDMARDs), which may not account for increasing bDMARD use. Annual dispensing data were used as a proxy for unique cases, which may have resulted in double‐counting of individuals who used a bDMARD over multiple years. The third, using the Medicine Insight Database, analysed de‐identified data from the electronic medical records of GP practices and calculated an RA prevalence of 0.9%; however, it included polymyalgia rheumatica in the RA definition. Finally, the oldest national data on Australian RA prevalence derive from the 1978–1982 National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC) twin registry, which had a moderate risk of bias due to non‐response rates, identifying 186 RA cases, with a prevalence of 0.4%. Discussion This is the first systematic review and meta‐analysis of vasculitis, SLE, RA, SSc, IIM, SpA, SjD and MCTD incidence or prevalence in Australia, highlighting the challenges of generating high‐quality data for rare diseases with nuanced diagnostic criteria. Three research gaps were identified. First, prevalence/incidence data are limited for non‐ANCA‐associated vasculitis, SpA, RA, SLE in SA, MCTD and SjD. In those SARDs with existing prevalence/incidence estimates, there remains a paucity of data from some population groups, with limited studies in the paediatric population and Australians of Asian descent. Second, validation studies could strengthen the use of Australian administrative health data for SARD research. Finally, geographic variation in AAV, SLE and SSc prevalence may be considerable but requires further investigation. Data on non‐ANCA‐associated vasculitis was limited, precluding meta‐analysis. Despite their relative frequency globally, , Australian data on SpA and PsA data are scarce. One WA study examined AS, one large primary care‐based study examined SpA but was limited by a fairly broad disease definition and PsA has been examined in a single, small Aboriginal community. SpA may be suited for analysis using Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS) data. Whilst 10 studies reported RA prevalence, most had data limitations. Like SpA, RA is well‐suited to administrative data due to its characteristic medications, with a PBS algorithm proposed and partially validated. Most SLE studies were from NA, limiting national generalisability. We estimated SLE prevalence in NA to be 57.86 (33.12–89.19) per 100 000, higher than a recent global estimate of 43.7 per 100 000, but lower than contemporary US (65–81 per 100 000 ) or UK (97–107 per 100 000 , ) estimates. This may reflect under‐ascertainment, as most studies were over a decade old, relying on a single hospital or clinician sources, supplemented with manual case‐finding (see Section S3.1). Despite these limitations, existing data show that First Nations peoples are disproportionately affected, with SLE prevalence reaching 91.24 (52.72–139.92) per 100 000, reinforcing the need to reduce autoimmune disease severity experienced by First Nations Australians. , , To refine national SLE prevalence estimates, research must use more rigorous case‐finding, expand beyond the Northern Territory and Far North Queensland and examine other at‐risk groups including Australians of Asian descent. , The two studies examining Asian Australians reported an LN prevalence of 27.9 and 64.3 per 100 000, far exceeding the Australian estimate of 11.2 per 100 000. , Administrative health data support comprehensive case identification through population‐wide coverage and were used in multiple studies. , , , , , , , Limitations include inaccuracies and limitations in coverage, so administrative data are ideally validated against confirmed cases and non‐cases. Internationally, validation studies have assessed algorithms for RA, SLE, SpA, , , vasculitis and IIM identification, but administrative databases vary by jurisdiction; thus, such validation studies are not directly applicable to Australia. Only one Australian study validating administrative data for SARD research was identified, which reviewed ICD coding for RA in WA. Concordance between administrative and biopsy‐based studies of LN suggests administrative data may be a valid tool for LN identification. Six of seven studies used renal biopsy databases; one used ICD‐coded hospital admissions, with similar results to a biopsy‐based study from the same region. Biopsy registries were also commonly used for case ascertainment in AAV and IIM studies. Half of the AAV studies used renal biopsy databases. Although histopathology (e.g. lung, renal or ear/nose/throat biopsies) is the diagnostic gold standard, a Dutch study found that only 45% of AAV patients underwent renal biopsies, despite glomerulonephritis being reported in 65%. , The renal biopsy rate among the Australian AAV population is unknown, which could lead to an underestimation of incidence. The recent launch of the Australian and New Zealand Vasculitis Quality and Disease Registry (ANZVASC‐QDR) will strengthen future research. As muscle biopsies are often reported at only a few laboratories, some studies screened all muscle biopsies in a given state for IIM case‐finding. , , , However, the 2017 European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology/American College of Rheumatology (EULAR/ACR) criteria do not require muscle biopsy, particularly for adults with typical skin manifestations. Furthermore, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was not included in the EULAR/ACR classification criteria; however, there has been increasing interest in the role of MRI as a diagnostic tool to guide biopsy or, when combined with other clinical features, to be used in place of biopsy. The addition of MRI criteria to the EULAR/ACR criteria applied to a cohort of Australian patients resulted in improved diagnostic accuracy, even when biopsy was not used, compared to the original EULAR/ACR criteria. The proportion of patients currently diagnosed with IIM in Australia without a biopsy is unknown, however. A 1999 Victorian study found that 8.5% of IIM patients had no biopsy, and a 2007 SA study identified that 32% of DM (not IIM) patients had no biopsy, and including non‐biopsied hospitalised patients doubled the DM incidence estimates, from 1.4 to 2.9 per million person‐years. Improved availability and awareness of the role of MRI and extended antibody panels may mean biopsies are even less frequent now; thus, relying on biopsy data alone may underestimate prevalence. This may differ by subtype, as the importance of histological confirmation varies; for example, IBM lacks reliably associated autoantibodies and often requires biopsy for diagnosis. Some studies supplemented biopsy data by also sending letters to all relevant clinicians. , Given the heterogeneity of IIM and involvement of multiple specialties, these methods are logistically challenging. , As an alternative, administrative data offer broader coverage but come with challenges. IIM epidemiology is particularly difficult due to evolving classification systems, and ICD‐based case identification without clinical review can lead to overestimation in the case of DM and PM. In the case of IBM, ICD coding likely results in underestimation as there is no specific ICD‐10 code for IBM. These challenges underscore the value of establishing a national Australian IIM registry to facilitate research efforts and the potential role for MRI data as a source of case identification. Geographic variation in disease frequency was reported in some studies of AAV, , SLE, IIM and SSc, , while others identified no geographic clustering. , This inconsistency may reflect weak geographic effects or selection bias. Random variation can cause some regions to appear to have higher or lower prevalence by chance, and clinician‐led studies may be biased toward areas with an observed excess of cases. When combined with small sample sizes, this effect can mimic true geographic differences. If SARD clusters do exist in Australia, they may be driven by local environmental exposures or regional demographic differences. Proposed exposures include silica dust (mining, quarrying, agriculture, forestry and construction), organic solvents and other chemicals. , , , , , National research using spatial statistics , may help to clarify these patterns. Strengths and limitations The strengths of this paper are that it is based on a systematic literature search, informed by the JBI guidance and Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta‐Analyses (PRISMA) statement, and used a validated tool for appraising prevalence study bias. Limitations relate to the underlying data, particularly the number of regionally based studies, which may limit generalisability. While inclusion of overlapping studies mostly had minimal impact on pooled estimates, in some cases the effect was material, necessitating their exclusion. This further reduced the number of studies available for meta‐analysis and underscores the uneven geographic distribution of research across Australia, with some regions studied multiple times and others not at all. Additionally, certain population groups remain under‐represented, including paediatric populations and Australians of different ethnic backgrounds. Most pooled estimates broadly aligned with international data, except SSc, where our estimate (25.58 per 100 000) exceeded the estimate for Australia (6.69 per 100 000) reported in a recent global meta‐analysis. The international estimate was based on three studies , , as opposed to our nine, as conference abstracts, , , registry studies , and regional studies were excluded. We are therefore confident in the robustness of our SSc estimate despite the difference from the global meta‐analysis. Conclusion This paper provides pooled incidence or prevalence estimates for AAV, SLE, LN, SSc, IIM and IBM, contributing to a growing body of SARD research in Australia. We identified three opportunities for future research. First, there are limited data on the prevalence of non‐ANCA‐associated vasculitis, RA, SpA, SjD and MCTD in Australia and a general paucity of studies on SARD prevalence in the paediatric population and Australians of diverse ethnic backgrounds. Second, there are few validation studies of Australian administrative health data for SARD research. Third, given the challenge of accurately identifying true geographic clusters of a rare disease, larger studies using spatial statistics are needed to identify clusters, in turn yielding aetiological clues.
